Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that make me feel strong emotions
I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred
Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I have lost my connection to my community and culture
I have permanently changed for the worse

vignette:
Amina, a thirty-five-year-old police officer, describes her life as having split into two distinct periods: before and after the assault. The six months since the attack have felt like a lifetime of steady, quiet erosion. The incident occurred while she was off-duty, responding to what she thought was a simple noise complaint from a neighbour in her apartment building. The man who answered the door recognized her from the community. The memory of what happened next is a fractured thing, a series of punishing snapshots rather than a coherent narrative. She remembers the initial shock, the sudden violence, but there are large portions of the event that are simply gone, voids she cannot fill no matter how desperately she tries. What remains comes back without warning. Sometimes it is the searing rage that floods her so completely she has to pull her patrol car over, gripping the wheel until the feeling passes. Other times, it is a physical haunting: a sharp, debilitating pain that blossoms in her wrists and jaw, an exact echo of where he held her down.

In the weeks that followed, Amina found herself consumed by a litany of "if onlys." She would lie awake for hours, replaying the moments leading up to the attack, certain that if she had only called for on-duty backup, if she had only been more suspicious, if she had only been stronger, life would not have fractured. This thought became a constant companion, the conviction that another woman, another officer, would not have gotten into that situation. She had come to believe she was uniquely weak, fundamentally flawed. This belief began to poison her perception of herself, corroding the pride she once took in her uniform and her strength. She felt permanently damaged, as if a vital part of her had been broken and could never be mended. This sense of being irrevocably changed created a chasm between her and the world she once knew.

Her life began to shrink. The boisterous family gatherings within her Nigerian community, once a source of deep comfort and connection, now felt unbearable. The laughter and easy conversation seemed to belong to a different world, one she could no longer access. She felt like an impostor among them, her secret shame a wall between her and her culture, and so she started making excuses to stay home. At work, a place that had once been her proving ground, she became a shadow of her former self. She began avoiding any call that hinted at a domestic dispute or any situation that might escalate into a confrontation. Her partner started giving her concerned looks when she would hesitate to exit the vehicle or let him take the lead in situations she would have once commanded. This avoidance wasn't a conscious strategy at first, just an instinct to steer clear of anything that might stir the violent, overwhelming emotions simmering just beneath the surface. Her marriage suffered from the same retreat; when her husband would try to talk about her silences, she would shut down, unable to bear the emotional intensity of his concern.

It was a performance review that finally forced her to seek help. Her sergeant, a man she respected, sat her down and spoke of a noticeable change in her conduct, a hesitation that was becoming a liability. The conversation was gentle, but for Amina, it was a confrontation she could not avoid. It made her realize that her attempts to manage her inner world were destroying her outer one. She was losing her job, her marriage, and her connection to her community, all in a desperate effort to contain a pain that refused to be contained. She is now terrified that her belief is true—that she is permanently broken—but a small, exhausted part of her hopes that she might one day feel like herself again, or at least learn to live with the person she has become.
